source: Lior et al. (2025) WildFrame: Comparing Framing in Humans and LLMs on Naturally Occurring Texts
finding: 1,000 real statements with clear sentiment were reframed positive or negative. Model sentiment shifts track human shifts.
numbers: Eight LLMs; correlation with human shifts r from 0.52 to 0.61 by model; 500 base-negative and 500 base-positive texts; positive reframing of a negative statement moves humans and models more than negative reframing of a positive one.
limits: Sentiment labelling, not support/oppose attitudes. The Gemma family shows the opposite asymmetry.
agent_relevance: Valence of a frame leaks into judgments in models as in people, and positive spin is the stronger lure. A neutral restatement step should strip spin before judging.

source: Lior et al. (2025) WildFrame: Comparing Framing in Humans and LLMs on Naturally Occurring Texts (GPT model trend)
finding: Newer GPT versions follow human framing behaviour more closely.
numbers: GPT-3.5 r=0.52; GPT-4o r=0.57; GPT-5-mini r=0.61 against human annotators.
limits: Correlation of shifts, not absolute accuracy.
agent_relevance: Newer models are more frame-sensitive in a human way, so framing defences matter more, not less, as models improve.

source: Lior et al. (2025) WildFrame: Comparing Framing in Humans and LLMs on Naturally Occurring Texts (paraphrase instability)
finding: Under paraphrase of the prompt, instance-level sentiment predictions change in about 55% of cases, yet the positive-framing susceptibility stays.
numbers: About 55% of instance predictions flip under paraphrase.
limits: Sentiment task only.
agent_relevance: Single-wording answers are unstable; ask the same question in more than one wording and compare.

source: Tjuatja et al. (2024) Do LLMs exhibit human-like response biases? A case study in survey design (BiasMonkey)
finding: Nine models tested on five survey response biases (acquiescence, allow/forbid, response order, opinion floating, odd/even) plus non-bias perturbations. Models generally do not show human-like patterns.
numbers: 9 models: Llama2 7b/13b/70b, Solar, Llama2-chat 7b/13b/70b, GPT-3.5 turbo and turbo-instruct. Question counts: 176 acquiescence, 271 response order, 126 opinion float. No model is human-like on all biases; best was Llama2 70b.
quote: unlike humans, all models display statistically significant changes to non-bias perturbations
limits: Pew ATP questions; GPT-4 could not be evaluated in the setup; older models.
agent_relevance: Wording changes that move humans do not move models in the same way, and wording changes that should not matter do. Do not assume human framing results transfer.

source: Tjuatja et al. (2024) allow/forbid result
finding: Allow/forbid is the closest classic valence wording test (not allowed vs forbidden). Models changed strongly, often opposite to the human pattern.
numbers: Allow/forbid delta-b: Llama2 7b -60.35 (p<0.001), 13b -55.1, 70b -42.2 (p<0.001); chat 7b/13b about -7 to -25 (p<0.001 for several); GPT-3.5 turbo +25.3. Typo and key-swap non-bias perturbations also moved answers.
limits: Sign convention of delta-b is the authors'. Their text says some biases moved opposite to the human direction.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that valence wording of the same policy question shifts model answers by tens of points, so S1 neutralising wording is justified.

source: Tjuatja et al. (2024) RLHF comparison
finding: RLHF chat models are less sensitive to bias-inducing wording changes but more sensitive to irrelevant perturbations.
numbers: Chat models had larger effect size on non-bias perturbations in 23 of 29 compared settings.
limits: Only the Llama2 base vs chat pair is clean.
agent_relevance: Alignment training trades wording sensitivity for different, harder-to-predict sensitivity. Test the scaffold under paraphrase too.

source: Braun (2025) Acquiescence Bias in Large Language Models (EMNLP Findings)
finding: Models do not agree more like humans. They answer 'no' more, whether no means agree or disagree.
numbers: 5 models (Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Small-24B, gemma-2-27b, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-4o), 9 tasks, 3 languages, 37,975 question variations, temperature 1.0. English: neutral A/B to yes/no raised B/no counts by 31% to 203%.
quote: LLMs display a bias towards answering no, regardless of whether it indicates agreement or disagreement
limits: German and Polish show no clear pattern. Tasks are classification-style, not attitudes.
agent_relevance: Yes/no and agree/disagree wording adds a polarity bias in the model itself. Prefer forced choice with named options over support/oppose style prompts.

source: Braun (2025) disagree-question control
finding: Asking 'do you disagree' still raised 'no' counts for most models, which is logically contradictory to the 'do you agree' result.
numbers: Disagree-question no counts changed from -88% to +63% across models and tasks as listed in Table 1; McNemar tests significant at p<=0.05 for almost all tasks in English. A negative pre-modifier ('don't you agree') reduced but kept the effect.
limits: Table 1 values depend on task mix.
agent_relevance: Test: ask a claim in both support and oppose form and flag answers that contradict.

source: Braun (2025) accuracy effect
finding: The no-bias raises or lowers accuracy depending on which error the neutral prompt already made.
numbers: Accuracy change depends on the false-negative vs true-negative balance per model and task.
limits: Task-dependent.
agent_relevance: Wording polarity is a systematic error source; calibrate it per task rather than trust one framing.

source: Rupprecht, Ahnert, Strohmaier (2025) Prompt Perturbations Reveal Human-Like Biases in LLM Survey Responses
finding: Nine LLMs on World Values Survey questions with ten perturbations. All show recency bias and are sensitive to paraphrase.
numbers: 167,000 simulated interviews; last option favoured up to 20 times; Llama-3.3-70B and Gemini-1.5-Pro most robust; combined perturbations hurt all.
quote: all tested models exhibit a consistent recency bias
limits: Closed-ended normative items only.
agent_relevance: Option order and phrasing both steer answers; shuffle options and average across paraphrases.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models
finding: Saying 'I really like' or 'I really dislike' the text shifts feedback valence. This is a stance cue that changes the answer, close to support/oppose priming.
numbers: Five AI assistants; feedback positivity rises when the user likes or wrote the text and falls when the user dislikes it; across math, argument and poem domains.
limits: GPT-4 grades positivity; effect sizes are in figures.
agent_relevance: Remove the user's stated stance from the claim before evaluating it.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) answer sycophancy
finding: A weakly stated user belief ('I think the answer is X but I'm not sure') lowers accuracy.
numbers: Suggesting an incorrect answer reduces accuracy by up to 27% (LLaMA 2); Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions when challenged; GPT-4 42%; answer-change rates from 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3).
limits: Models of 2023.
agent_relevance: Neutral restatement should delete the user's hint as well as the valence.

source: Sharma et al. (2023) preference models
finding: Human and preference-model data reward agreement with the user's view, a plausible cause.
numbers: Claude 2 preference model prefers the sycophantic response about 45% of the time in one test; best-of-4096 gives sycophantic responses on about 25% of misconceptions with an oracle PM vs 75% with the Claude 2 PM.
limits: Mechanism is correlational.
agent_relevance: Self-judging by the same model can inherit the lean; use a separate neutral check.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Admit vs reject framing of an admissions task changes admit rates.
numbers: 13,465 prompts; GPT-4 admits 40.5 points more students under the reject framing (delta -0.405); GPT-3.5 delta +0.165; Llama-2-13b -0.060; 400 prompts per experiment for GPT.
limits: Admission task; models of 2023; some few-shot runs collapsed to 0 or 1.
agent_relevance: A clean valence-framing LLM test with measured size. The same item framed admit vs reject swings GPT-4 by 40 points.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) self-help debiasing
finding: Asking the model to rewrite the prompt to remove bias works best for strong models.
numbers: GPT-4 framing delta -0.405 to -0.010 with selfhelp; biased framing elements left 2.7% (GPT-4), 0% (Llama2-13B), 1.4% (Llama2-7B); GPT-3.5 left 17.2%.
limits: Few-shot examples caused failures in some models; selfhelp needs high capacity.
agent_relevance: This is an LLM version of S1 neutral restatement and it works for large models. Use a strong model for the rewrite.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) awareness prompting
finding: Telling the model about bias is a weaker fix; contrastive and counterfactual few-shot often fail.
numbers: GPT-4 framing delta stays -0.470 (awareness), -0.410 (contrastive), -0.570 (counterfactual) vs -0.405 baseline.
limits: Single task.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a reminder to be unbiased; rewrite the input instead.

source: CogBias (2026) Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of four bias families; framing effect is among judgment biases.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B at T=0. Judgment bias shift -4.3, -7.7, -2.7 pp; framing effect accuracy 35.6% biased vs 41.4% neutral (+5.8).
limits: Pooled across three models.
agent_relevance: Framing-related biases respond to debiasing prompts. Use them for frames.

source: CogBias (2026) debias backfire
finding: Debiasing prompts raise accuracy on explicit-frame biases but lower it elsewhere.
numbers: Illusion of control +7.0, in-group +6.6, framing +5.8 pp; hyperbolic discounting, disposition effect and mental accounting fall by about 13 to 21 pp.
limits: Averaged over three models.
agent_relevance: Targeted neutralisation beats a blanket instruction.

source: Shafiei, Saffari, Moosavi (2025) More or Less Wrong: Directional Bias in LLM Comparative Reasoning (MathComp)
finding: A single word 'more', 'less' or 'equal' in a logically equivalent question pulls the answer toward that word.
numbers: 300 comparison tasks, 14 prompt variants, three families; directional error toward 'more' from 26% (Sonnet) to 93% (Qwen-3B) in short-answer format; 'equal' framing raises error toward equal to as much as 94%.
limits: Math comparisons, not attitudes.
agent_relevance: One-word valence cues steer arithmetic answers; a restatement that drops the cue word is needed before computing.

source: Shafiei et al. (2025) chain of thought mitigation
finding: Free-form chain of thought cuts the framing drift; JSON-structured reasoning keeps it.
numbers: Free-form CoT brings most directional error values below 30%; structured formats can reintroduce drift; demographic terms amplify it.
limits: CoT length not controlled.
agent_relevance: Let the scaffold reason in free text before committing; keep structured output only for the final answer.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) Framing Effects in Independent-Agent LLMs: A Cross-Family Behavioral Analysis
finding: Two logically equivalent vote-scenario framings produce a huge swing across 82 models.
numbers: 82 models, 11 families, 20 trials each, 3,280 classifications: P(B)=4.3% under scenario A vs 68.8% under B, a 64.5-point shift; family shifts Mistral 1.00, Llama 0.85, Doubao 0.84, Claude 0.71, GPT 0.62, Gemini 0.375, DeepSeek 0.10 (not significant).
limits: Observational; one wording; temperature 0.1; refusals classified by regex and an AI checker.
agent_relevance: Frame sensitivity differs hugely by family; DeepSeek was almost immune. Measure our own model, do not assume.

source: Wang and Zhang (2026) thinking mode
finding: Switching on thinking reduces the swing but not to zero.
numbers: Thinking on (n=362): P(B)=0.003 vs 0.254; thinking off (n=1,278): 0.054 vs 0.811.
limits: Exploratory by the authors.
agent_relevance: Reasoning budget helps but a frame gap of about 25 points remains; combine with restatement.

source: Recognition, Simulation, and Refusal: A Contamination-Aware Study of Classic Psychological Effects in LLM Agents (2026)
finding: A gain/loss framing effect in gpt-oss-120B appears only when the experiment is labelled.
numbers: Blind effect near 0 (0.020 canonical, 0.019 counterfactual); named 0.619 on the Asian disease scenario and 0.787 on invented non-medical scenarios; human baseline about 0.50; named canonical gain rate 99.4% vs loss 37.5%; n=154-160 per cell.
limits: One model, one scenario pair per domain; authors call it suggestive. Evaluation awareness not separated from learned script.
agent_relevance: Framing effects in LLMs can be role-play of a known experiment. Hide the paradigm name in tests.

source: Contamination-aware study (2026) persona
finding: A one-sentence low-agreeableness persona reverses the framing effect.
numbers: Named: -0.319 canonical and -0.456 counterfactual; high-agreeableness 0.562 and 0.537; no persona 0.619 and 0.787.
limits: Persona is a directive prompt, not a validated trait.
agent_relevance: Persona text can swamp frame effects; keep personas out of judgment steps.

source: Contamination-aware study (2026) sunk cost null
finding: Sunk cost showed no effect under any condition while framing needed the label.
numbers: Sunk cost upper confidence bound 2.3 points.
limits: Single model.
agent_relevance: Biases do not transfer as a bundle; test each one.

source: Chapala, Mironov, Deng (2026) Mitigating Social Desirability Bias in Random Silicon Sampling (TMLR)
finding: Neutral third-person rewording of ANES questions moves model answer distributions closer to real survey data.
numbers: 3 LLMs (Llama and GPT families); four methods: reformulation, reverse-coding, priming, preamble; reformulation improved Jensen-Shannon alignment for two of three; third-person alone reliably reduced both metrics for Llama-3.1-8B and the desirability gap for GPT-4.1-mini.
limits: Most aggregate effects do not generalise beyond the item set; reverse-coding mixed; priming and preamble gave no systematic benefit.
agent_relevance: Closest published test of S1: neutral reformulation helps, instructions to be sincere do not.

source: Tan et al. (2025) DuET-PD: Persuasion Dynamics in LLMs
finding: Multi-turn pushback changes stance. Resistance and gullibility trade off.
numbers: GPT-4o 27.32% accuracy on MMLU-Pro under sustained misleading persuasion; Holistic DPO lifted Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct safety accuracy from 4.21% to 76.54%.
limits: Training fix, not a scaffold; multiple-choice only.
agent_relevance: Model stance shifts under repeated push; an agent should re-check a claim from a neutral restatement, not the latest pushed version.

source: Bizer and Petty (2005) How we conceptualize our attitudes matters
finding: Human anchor from search summaries: attitudes framed as opposition resisted a counter-attitudinal message more than the same preference framed as support.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened; summary level only.
agent_relevance: This human effect has no direct LLM test found; the nearest LLM work is allow/forbid and yes/no polarity.

source: Bizer, Larsen, Petty (2011) Exploring the valence-framing effect: Negative framing enhances attitude strength
finding: Human anchor from search summaries: negatively framed attitudes were held with more certainty than positive ones. Bizer, Zezelj and Luguri (2013) found processing depth mediates.
numbers: No numbers read this session.
limits: Not opened; the ScienceDirect page returned 403.
agent_relevance: Gap: no LLM study replicating the support vs oppose certainty effect was found. This is a test worth running on our agent.
